subject: gargoyle
pitch:
Category: Monster.
Subject: cathedral gargoyle crouched on a ledge.
Style: gothic stone carving.
reasoning:
I'm planning a full module for a crouching gothic stone gargoyle, aiming for a substantial build with the proper SDK imports and helper functions for shapes, geometry, and painting.

I'm sketching the scene geometry: a stone ledge block with moulding at roughly knee height, and a gargoyle crouched on top with haunches raised, wings half-spread like a bat's, and arms extended forward onto the ledge, all facing +Z with glowing ember eyes.

I'm working through the skeleton chain now, placing hip, spine, chest, neck, and head joints with specific coordinates to capture that hunched crouching posture with the head lifted and shoulders rounded forward.

Now I'm figuring out the arm placement from shoulders down to hands gripping the ledge, then moving to legs with a digitigrade-style thigh-shin-foot setup for the crouched stance.

I'm computing the knee position by orthogonalizing the bend hint against the hip-ankle chord direction, then offsetting the midpoint by the perpendicular distance to get the knee at roughly (0.21, 0.57, 0.02).

That height seems too close to the hip though, making it look crouched rather than natural, so I should splay the knees outward with an x-component in the hint and shorten the leg segments to around 0.26 each. I'll structure each leg as a three-joint chain (hip, knee, ankle) with the ankle as the tip, then attach separate toe chains branching off the ankle for the foot.

I'm sketching a helper function for a clawed foot that builds a box for the ankle plus three toe capsules with claw spikes per foot, positioning the toes forward from the ankle so they rest just above the ledge surface.

For the arms, I'm computing shoulder-to-wrist distances and bend directions to figure elbow hints, then planning three large claw-like fingers per hand positioned near the front edge of the ledge as if gripping it.

Now I'm working out the head placement and orientation, building a neck chain from base to head joint and deciding the skull faces slightly downward and forward in a glaring stance typical of a gargoyle.

I'll build the neck as a short chain from the spine base to the head pivot point, then attach the head joint to the neck tip with a jaw joint beneath it. For the spine I'm planning a loft from tail through hips to chest, with the tail curving backward and down off the body.

Now I'm working out the tail's curl along the ledge — path points sweeping from the hips outward and sideways, ending in a spade-shaped tip lying flat on the ledge surface, and sizing the ledge itself (width, depth, and a two-tier block with a slightly overhanging cornice) so there's enough room for the tail and wingspan.

I'm deciding to keep decoration restrained — a corbel row under the front edge and a quatrefoil panel carved into the face via texture — and skipping a back wall since the tail already fits within the ledge depth, then moving on to plan the bat wings and the shoulder/arm joint positions.

Now I'm working out the wing geometry: placing the elbow and wrist joints outward and upward from the shoulder, fanning finger bones from the wrist with webbing between them, and checking that the spread tips and drooping fingers clear the ledge top so nothing intersects the stonework.

Setting up membrane generation between finger chains, resampling edges by arc length since both start at the wrist and converge at the root, which creates a degenerate point there.

Both edges should start at the wrist—one running outward to the fingertip, the other inward toward the body/hip—so they share a consistent root-to-tip direction. For the body-side points without explicit bone bindings, I'll let them default to the nearest joint.

I'll give edge A its own joint chain and pass a spine/chest joint as the bone reference for edge B, following the convention that path edges follow a joint chain when `bone` is specified. For the wing membranes, I'll connect between the finger chains (f1–f2, f2–f3, f3–f4) and from f4 to the body, using scalloped edges and a lighter, finer-grained stone texture for the membrane versus thicker, darker stone for the finger bones themselves, with membrane thickness set to 0.025.

Tallying joints: each wing has an arm chain (3 joints) plus four two-joint fingers (8), giving 11 joints per side, doubled for both wings, plus legs at roughly 3 joints each side — all comfortably within the 160-joint budget. Now I'm laying out the full skeleton: a root hips joint, then a spine chain running from hips through mid-spine and chest to the neck base using a Catmull-Rom path (yielding default-named spine1–spine3), followed by a neck chain from the neck base to the head point (neck1, neck2) parented off the spine's last joint, with the head joint parented to the neck's final joint.

I'm also sketching a tail chain parented at hips with about six segments, plus leg and arm chains, and wing shoulders anchored near the chest joint. I'm roughing out spine coordinates and body proportions — back height around 0.7-0.9, shoulder width ±0.25, belly clearance above the ledge — then planning a loft shape along the spine path with wider hips, a tapered mid-section, and bulkier chest stations to give the body a heavy-shouldered, sagging-belly silhouette.

Now I'm reconsidering whether to use a sweep instead of a loft for a blockier, faceted stone look, using a faceted circular cross-section (roughly octagonal) with radius functions along the up/forward normals, and figuring out how the bone list (tail, hips, spine, head) should map onto that path given that the hips joint itself has no length.

I'm worried the hips-to-spine1 bone is zero length and that root joints without parents might break the chain logic, so I'm considering making the spine chain start slightly offset from hips, or just excluding hips from the body sweep and letting it begin at spine1's position while the tail gets its own separate sweep that buries its thick root into the body at the hip junction.

Now I'm defining the radius profile along the spine chain (narrower at hips, slightly tapering mid-back, widening at the chest, then narrowing again toward the neck base) and setting up a stone paint function that layers warm/cool lighting, moss on upward-facing surfaces, soot in crevices, weathering mottle, vertical rain streaks, and lichen patches using layered noise.

Writing noise-based paint logic...

Defining stone material variants...

Writing ashlar paint logic...

I'll use a sine-based hash for pseudo-randomness, keep flat colors minimal (amber eye glow, bone/stone teeth) since there's a 64-color limit, and rely on paints for most surfaces. Now I'm planning out the 5-12 textures needed, starting with the eye texture.

For the eyes, I'm deciding between carving sockets into the skull with a glowing eyeball sphere textured and lit via a glow effect, or using an outward-facing circle plane with the eye texture mapped onto it as a simpler alternative to sphere UV rotation issues.

I'm also figuring out the quatrefoil ledge panel as a tinted stone relief with dark outlines and highlights, and considering how to add carved rib patterns to the wing membranes using paint coordinates along the span and across the fingers since membranes only accept paint rather than textures.

For extra detail, I'm thinking about a chest emblem — maybe a small cathedral-style cross or trefoil roundel decal — plus moss and lichen tufts on the ledge and shoulders using card-based SVG textures.

Then I'm tallying additional surface details: an eye texture, a gothic arcade frieze trim along the ledge cornice, and thin crack decals scattered sparingly on the body for weathering. Counting it up, that's roughly six to seven distinct textures total (eye, quatrefoil, roundel, frieze, moss tuft, crack), which feels like enough variety without overdoing it, and I'm noting the eyes should carry an amber glow.

I'm deciding to keep the glow effect limited to the eyes only, since a gothic stone carving look calls for restraint -- a faint amber eye glow reads as a nice hero detail without breaking the stone aesthetic, so I'll skip mouth embers or lit lanterns. Now I'm working out the head geometry, defining a head pivot point and center offset from the neck joint so the jaw can be split into separate upper and lower parts, with a uniform head scale constant to tie the proportions together.
